column6: Pioneer Green Energy abandoned plans for a wind project in Etowah County after local residents filed a lawsuit and state restrictions were enacted.

column6: Local residents opposed a proposed solar farm in Covington County citing concerns about the impact on family properties and well water supplies.
column17: Local residents expressed strong opposition to a proposed 160-MW, 1,000-acre solar panel array at an August 21, 2023 meeting. The residents opposed the farm for several reasons, including that it would be powering communities over an hour away and not their own; that the solar farm might encroach on family properties that have existed for generations; and that potential road runoff might impact their well water supplies.

column6: Stop Wind Farms group opposed the 180-MW Nimbus Wind Farm in Carroll County, Arkansas.
column17: In 2016, Scout Clean Energy began negotiating contracts with landowners for the 180-MW Nimbus Wind Farm, which would cover 14 square miles of land atop the Ozark Mountains. In 2023, a group called Stop Wind Farms was formed to oppose this development and collected over 1,000 verified signatures in opposition, raising concerns about disturbances to the aesthetic value of the Ozark ridgeline and decreased property values. Nevertheless, on September 17, 2024, the Carroll County Quorum Court approved Scout to use county roads for installation, so long as Scout covered the cost for road maintenance around the wind farm.
column19: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

column6: Protect Our Pocketbooks opposed the Wind Catcher Energy Connection Project in Washington County, Arkansas.
column17: In July 2018, American Electric Power abandoned plans to build a $4.5 billion, 2,000-MW wind farm in the Oklahoma panhandle, as well as an associated interstate transmission project that would have delivered electricity to Arkansas and other states. In Arkansas, a dark money group called Protect Our Pocketbooks paid for television advertisements claiming that Arkansas would receive no benefits from the project. The developer responded by issuing a statement that Protect Our Pocketbooks was “presenting misleading information to the public, including manipulation of statements by Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson.” Although the Arkansas Public Service Commission ultimately granted approval for the Arkansas components of the project, the Wind Catcher project was canceled altogether when the Texas Public Service Commission denied approval.
column19: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

column6: Nature and People First sought to develop a utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project, facing opposition from local residents and environmental groups.
column17: The developer Nature and People First has sought to develop a 6,000-MW, utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project on approximately 400 acres of land in Apache and Navajo Counties. In July 2023, three organizations submitted a letter to FERC attaching resolutions against the project from 18 Navajo Nation chapters and agencies. Nearby residents had expressed concerns about potential damage to underground water supplies and sacred lands, and that the developer had not sufficiently involved nearby residents. In February 2024, FERC denied applications for a preliminary permit for the project.
column19: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

column6: The SunZia transmission line faced legal challenges from tribes and environmental groups over its routing in the San Pedro Valley.
column17: The SunZia transmission line, expected to open in 2026 with the ability to carry more than 3,600 MW of wind power generated in New Mexico wind farms, routed through the San Pedro Valley. The Tohono O’odham, Hopi, Zuni, and San Carlos Apache tribes claimed that the Bureau of Land Management ignored over 15 years of attempts by the tribes to recognize the valley as a culturally significant area. In January 2024, these tribes, along with Center for Biological Diversity and Archeology Southwest, filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona, claiming that the review of the project violated NEPA and the NHPA. The lawsuit was dismissed in June 2024 and subsequently appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.
column19: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

column3: Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area First-Generation Wind Farms
column6: A lawsuit was brought against the operators of wind turbines in Altamont Pass, alleging bird deaths.
column17: In 2004, the Center for Biological Diversity brought a lawsuit against the operators of wind turbines in the Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, alleging that the “obsolete, first-generation wind turbine generators” being used at the site were killing and injuring birds in violation of the public trust doctrine. The lawsuit was dismissed, and the dismissal was upheld on appeal.

column6: Local groups opposed two solar projects, leading to legal challenges and appeals.
column17: Opponents of two North Livermore Valley solar projects, Aramis (410 acres) and Sunwalker (70 acres), led by a group called Save North Livermore Valley, argued that the proposed locations of the projects impinge on agriculture, natural wildlife habitat, open space, and visual and scenic resources. In October 2020, two candidates running for election to the Alameda County Board of Supervisors issued a joint statement urging the board to place a moratorium on solar development on agricultural land. After the East County Board of Zoning Adjustments approved both projects, local groups stated appealed both decisions. By December 2020, three local organizations had filed appeals challenging the approval of the Aramis project. In May 2022, the Alameda County Superior Court upheld the county’s approval of the Aramis project, dismissing a lawsuit by project opponents. In July 2023, Save North Livermore Valley appealed the Superior Court’s decision. California’s First District Court of Appeals denied the appeal in August 2023.
column19: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

column6: Local community members opposed the Aratina Solar Center project due to wildlife and Joshua Tree concerns.
column17: In October 2021, the Kern County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the Aratina Solar Center, a solar-plus-storage project including 530 MW of solar capacity and 600 MW of battery energy storage capacity. Shortly thereafter, local community members organized a petition that received 51,000 signatures. A primary concern driving local opposition to the project is the potential impact on local wildlife and on Joshua Trees. In compliance with the California Western Joshua Tree Conservation Act, the developer received an Incidental Take Permit, which authorized the developer to remove trees with an option to pay a standard mitigation fee rather than complete mitigation fee.
column19: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

column6: The Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project faced legal challenges over government-to-government consultation.
column17: The Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project is a 465-MW solar farm built between 2010 and 2020 over 4,070 acres of BLM land by the developer NextEra. The Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) sued the Department of Interior in 2014 in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, claiming that BLM’s lack of government-to-government consultation violated the NHPA; the lawsuit also included claims under NEPA and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the Department of Interior in July 2015.
column19: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

column6: Residents challenged the Boulder Brush Project, alleging violations of environmental laws.
column17: The Boulder Brush Project is a 320-acre substation and transmission line proposed by Terra-Gen, which would connect to the 60-turbine Campo Wind Project planned for the Campo Indian Reservation. In March 2021, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the project. Residents consequently formed an organization called Backcountry Against Dumps to challenge the decision. In April 2021, the organization filed a lawsuit claiming that the project violated the California Environmental Quality Act and various planning and zoning regulations. The lawsuit contended that the County’s environmental review of the project did not fully analyze the risks to wildlife and groundwater and the effects of noise disruptions. In March 2024, the Fourth District Court of Appeal vacated the San Diego Superior Court’s dismissal of the lawsuit, instructing the trial court to allow the case to proceed.

column6: The Alta Wind Farm faced local opposition and legal challenges but eventually began operation in 2023.
column8: court_ruling: Alta Farms Wind Project II v. DeWitt County
column17: The 200-MW Alta Wind Farm was approved in July 2020 by the DeWitt County Board despite local opposition. The project had been proposed nearly 10 years before. In July 2021, the DeWitt County Board approved a motion preventing the issuance of new building permits to Enel Green Power for the Alta Wind Farm until the company could prove that its turbines could be curtailed during severe weather events. An Illinois judge then issued a mandamus order holding that the Dewitt County Board lacked legal authority to halt the issuance of building permits. The wind farm proceeded to operation in June 2023.

Local residents opposed the project due to concerns about aesthetic changes, wildlife impacts, and groundwater contamination.
